content: India has been actively promoting the cultivation of Jatropha curcas as part of its strategy to achieve energy independence by 2012. Jatropha oil, derived from the seeds of the Jatropha plant, is considered an excellent source of biodiesel. This plant thrives in wastelands across India, making it a viable option for large-scale cultivation. The Indian government aims to reduce its reliance on coal and petroleum to meet the country's growing energy demands, and Jatropha cultivation is a key element of this policy. Vast tracts of wasteland have been earmarked for Jatropha farming, which is expected to provide employment opportunities for the rural poor. Additionally, businesses view Jatropha cultivation as a lucrative investment. The government has identified 400,000 square kilometers (98 million acres) of land suitable for Jatropha cultivation, with the goal of replacing 20% of India's diesel consumption by 2011. Dr. Abdul Kalam, the former President of India, has been a strong advocate for Jatropha cultivation to produce biodiesel. In a recent speech, he highlighted that out of the 60 million hectares of wasteland available in India, over 30 million hectares are suitable for Jatropha farming. Once planted, Jatropha has a productive lifespan of several decades and requires minimal water compared to other cash crops. The State Bank of India has supported this initiative by signing an agreement with D1 Mohan to provide loans worth 1.3 billion rupees to local farmers. Farmers can repay these loans using the income generated from selling Jatropha seeds to D1 Mohan. The Indian Railways has successfully begun using Jatropha oil blended with diesel to power its locomotives. Diesel engines operating on routes such as Thanjavur to Nagore and Tiruchirapalli to Lalgudi, Dindigul, and Karur are now running on this biodiesel blend. In Andhra Pradesh, the state government has partnered with Reliance Industries to cultivate Jatropha on 200 acres of land in Kakinada for high-quality biodiesel production. Similarly, Kerala is planning a large-scale Jatropha planting campaign. Chhattisgarh has launched an ambitious plan to plant 160 million Jatropha saplings across its 16 districts by 2006, aiming to become a biofuel self-reliant state by 2015. The state expects to generate Rs 40 billion annually from seed sales after 2010. The central government has allocated Rs 135 million to Chhattisgarh for developing Jatropha nurseries. In May 2005, Chief Minister Raman Singh became the first state leader to use Jatropha biodiesel in his official vehicle. The state plans to transition all government vehicles from diesel and petrol to Jatropha biodiesel by 2007. The Chhattisgarh Biofuel Development Authority oversees the production of Jatropha seeds as a biodiesel source. In Karnataka, farmers in semi-arid regions are increasingly planting Jatropha due to its suitability for such conditions. For instance, a coconut farmer near Bangalore, B.K. Nagendrappa, has expressed interest in planting up to 12 acres of Jatropha on his land. Tamil Nadu is aggressively promoting Jatropha cultivation to help farmers mitigate losses caused by irregular rainfall in recent years. The state government has partnered with four companies—Mohan Breweries and Distilleries Limited, Shiva Distilleries Limited, Dharani Sugars and Chemicals Limited, and Riverway Agro Products Private Ltd—to develop Jatropha plantations on a large scale. Currently, these companies have cultivated Jatropha on 3 square kilometers of land, with a target of 50 square kilometers. The Tamil Nadu government has also abolished the purchase tax on Jatropha to encourage its cultivation. Rajasthan is an ideal location for Jatropha cultivation due to its minimal water requirements, which align with the state's arid conditions. Jatropha plantations have been established in districts such as Udaipur, Kota, Sikar, Banswara, Chittor, and Churu. In Udaipur, Jatropha is being grown in agroforestry systems alongside food or cash crops on marginal lands. The plant's toxic leaves make it unpalatable to livestock, ensuring the saplings remain intact. In Maharashtra, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) has partnered with the Maharashtra State Farming Corporation Ltd (MSFCL) to develop a Jatropha-based biodiesel project. The initiative includes cultivating Jatropha on 500 acres in Nashik and Aurangabad. In November 2005, the Maharashtra government set a goal to cultivate Jatropha on 600 square kilometers of land, with half allocated to the public sector and the other half to the private sector. Pune Municipal Corporation became a pioneer in using Jatropha biodiesel in over 100 public buses starting July 1, 2006. In Ahmednagar, Gulabrao Kale spearheaded efforts to promote Jatropha cultivation under the DPAP (Drought Prone Area Programme). Initially, convincing farmers to adopt Jatropha farming was challenging due to low literacy levels and skepticism about the plant's potential benefits. However, after persistent efforts, over 1,000 farmers are now participating in the program. Under the watershed development initiative, the Govind Gramin Vikas Pratishthan (GOGVIP) has planted more than 2 million Jatropha plants across 1,092 hectares in five villages: Vankute, Dhoki, Dhotre, Dhavalpuri, and Gajdipoor. These villages are in remote areas, making it difficult to establish connections with GOGVIP, but the program has successfully overcome these challenges.
